attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in his own post, given as his third reason. They are not the diplomat's paraphrase.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the claim of a sycophantic tendency. 'Greatest ever' is rightly read as rhetorical exaggeration. Leaving out 'well-known' is harmless, and the contract restores it through earlier research.

contract.note: The plain reading (a recurring pattern of unwarranted praise or agreement, not in every response) is fair and ordinary. Picking March 2026 as the period to test a present-tense tendency is reasonable.

evidence.note: Dated March 2026 snapshot. It keeps the dispute fixed and swaps the narrator, and finds sycophantic contradictions in every one of the 16 configurations. Rates vary widely, and contrarian errors also occur, which limits how widespread the pattern is.
Anthropic research from 2023 showing sycophancy was already documented, so the tendency was well known. It is a company paper about earlier systems, not a measurement for the target period.

reviews.rationale: A controlled March 2026 evaluation found agreement that followed whoever was narrating, in all 16 model configurations tested. Earlier research shows the behaviour was already well known. Rates vary a lot and the benchmark tests agreement rather than flattery, but a tendency need not be universal. This meets the support condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, given as his first reason in his own post.

semantics.note: Marcus says the missing robust world models are why generative AI is not good at strategy, so a causal reading is faithful. The 'never' scope is kept.

contract.note: Marcus did not define 'robust world model', and he named no test linking such models to strategic skill. The contract's reading is reasonable, but the result depends on it.

evidence.note: 2024 study finding incoherent world models and fragility on narrow tasks. It suggests a plausible mechanism but says nothing about strategy or about systems up to April 2026.
The Othello study shows a model can form a causally useful internal representation in a toy domain. That qualifies 'never' in a narrow sense, but it is not robust understanding of the wider world.

reviews.rationale: Both studies are narrow and point in different directions. Neither covers the full range of generative systems up to April 2026, and nothing in the packet links world-model failures to poor strategic reasoning. The evidence does not settle the causal claim.

contract.note: The plain reading (a broad weakness at reliable transfer, not total inability) is fair. Marcus set no threshold for 'very good' and did not say what counts as a new situation, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: The ARC-AGI-3 report says frontier systems scored below 1% in March 2026 on new interactive environments that humans solve. The score measures efficiency against human baselines, not the share of tasks solved.

Google's own blog reports a verified 77.1% on ARC-AGI-2's new static puzzles before the post. This is a company disclosure, and possible training exposure is unresolved, but it does qualify 'never very good'.

reviews.rationale: The claim holds for new interactive environments: frontier systems scored below 1% on ARC-AGI-3 in March 2026. A verified 77.1% on ARC-AGI-2's static new-pattern tasks, though only company-reported, cuts against the blanket 'never been very good'.

OpenAI's own March 2026 announcement of better document and general work performance. It does not isolate memo quality or factual accuracy.

reviews.rationale: No readable evaluation in the packet tests whether March 2026 systems write adequate routine memos. The 2023 study is too early, and OpenAI's aggregate figures are its own disclosure. The evidence leans toward adequacy but does not meet the contract's requirements.
